Data inputs and inspection

Source: vignettes/data_import.Rmd
data_import.Rmd

recipe() accepts a phyloseq or TreeSummarizedExperiment object. These containers connect an abundance matrix to sample metadata and, when available, taxonomy. Import files with the tools supplied by phyloseq or mia, then inspect the resulting object before configuring an analysis.

Importing data does not establish that their units, experimental design or taxonomic annotations are appropriate for a particular differential-abundance method.

Start with an existing phyloseq object

The package includes metaHIV_phy, with its recorded sample metadata and taxonomy. No statistical model is needed to inspect the data or define preprocessing steps.

library(dar)
data("metaHIV_phy", package = "dar")

rec <- recipe(metaHIV_phy)
rec
#> ── DAR Recipe ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Inputs:
#> 
#>      ℹ phyloseq object with 451 taxa and 156 samples 
#>      ✖ undefined analysis target. Use add_model() to define the analysis! 
#>      ✖ undefined taxonomic level. Use add_model() to define the analysis!

recipe() also accepts a phyloseq object whose stored abundance matrix has samples in rows: the accessors below return one consistent orientation. When constructing your own phyloseq object, set taxa_are_rows to match the actual matrix, rather than changing this flag without transposing the data.

Inspect samples, taxonomy and abundances

Use the dar accessors explicitly when other attached packages export functions with the same names.

samples <- dar::sample_data(rec)
taxonomy <- dar::tax_table(rec)
abundances <- dar::otu_table(rec)

head(samples[c("sample_id", "RiskGroup2")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   sample_id  RiskGroup2
#>   <chr>      <chr>     
#> 1 Sample_186 msm       
#> 2 Sample_185 msm       
#> 3 Sample_184 hts       
#> 4 Sample_182 pwid      
#> 5 Sample_181 msm       
#> 6 Sample_170 msm
head(taxonomy)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   taxa_id Kingdom  Phylum         Class           Order     Family Genus Species
#>   <chr>   <chr>    <chr>          <chr>           <chr>     <chr>  <chr> <chr>  
#> 1 Otu_1   Archaea  Euryarchaeota  Methanobacteria Methanob… Metha… Meth… Methan…
#> 2 Otu_2   Archaea  Euryarchaeota  Methanobacteria Methanob… Metha… Meth… Methan…
#> 3 Otu_3   Bacteria Actinobacteria Actinobacteria  Actinomy… Actin… Acti… Actino…
#> 4 Otu_4   Bacteria Actinobacteria Actinobacteria  Actinomy… Actin… Acti… Actino…
#> 5 Otu_5   Bacteria Actinobacteria Actinobacteria  Actinomy… Actin… Acti… Actino…
#> 6 Otu_6   Bacteria Actinobacteria Actinobacteria  Actinomy… Actin… Acti… Actino…
abundances[seq_len(6), seq_len(5)]
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   taxa_id Sample_186 Sample_185 Sample_184 Sample_182
#>   <chr>        <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 Otu_1         2538          0       9026      12049
#> 2 Otu_2            0          0          0        609
#> 3 Otu_3            0          0          0          0
#> 4 Otu_4            0          0          0          0
#> 5 Otu_5            0          0          0          0
#> 6 Otu_6            0          0          0          0

The accessors expose the complete stored components, independently of the target or taxonomic rank later selected with add_model():

  • sample_data() returns sample_id followed by all sample metadata columns, in phyloseq::sample_names() order.
  • tax_table() returns taxa_id followed by all taxonomic ranks, in phyloseq::taxa_names() order.
  • otu_table() returns one row per taxon, with taxa_id first and one column per sample. Taxon and sample order match the other two accessors.
stopifnot(
  identical(colnames(abundances)[-1], samples$sample_id),
  identical(abundances$taxa_id, taxonomy$taxa_id)
)

Keep sample and taxon identifiers unique and consistent across input files. Taxonomic labels are annotations, not replacements for feature identifiers: several features can share a species name. Inspect missing annotations and use standard rank names such as Kingdom, Genus and Species.

If metadata or taxonomy is absent, the corresponding accessor returns an ID-only tibble. That is sufficient for inspection, but it does not supply the real covariates or taxonomic rank needed by a model. Add genuine study metadata before calling add_model(); do not manufacture groups just to make an example run.

Import a BIOM table

This example uses a file distributed with phyloseq, without downloading data. The importer reads the sample metadata already present in that file.

biom_file <- system.file(
  "extdata", "rich_dense_otu_table.biom", package = "phyloseq"
)

phy <- phyloseq::import_biom(
  biom_file,
  parseFunction = phyloseq::parse_taxonomy_greengenes
)
biom_rec <- recipe(phy)
head(dar::sample_data(biom_rec))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   sample_id BarcodeSequence LinkerPrimerSequence  BODY_SITE Description
#>   <chr>     <chr>           <chr>                 <chr>     <chr>      
#> 1 Sample1   CGCTTATCGAGA    CATGCTGCCTCCCGTAGGAGT gut       human gut  
#> 2 Sample2   CATACCAGTAGC    CATGCTGCCTCCCGTAGGAGT gut       human gut  
#> 3 Sample3   CTCTCTACCTGT    CATGCTGCCTCCCGTAGGAGT gut       human gut  
#> 4 Sample4   CTCTCGGCCTGT    CATGCTGCCTCCCGTAGGAGT skin      human skin 
#> 5 Sample5   CTCTCTACCAAT    CATGCTGCCTCCCGTAGGAGT skin      human skin 
#> 6 Sample6   CTAACTACCAAT    CATGCTGCCTCCCGTAGGAGT skin      human skin
head(dar::tax_table(biom_rec))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 8
#>   taxa_id  Kingdom  Phylum         Class              Order Family Genus Species
#>   <chr>    <chr>    <chr>          <chr>              <chr> <chr>  <chr> <chr>  
#> 1 GG_OTU_1 Bacteria Proteobacteria Gammaproteobacter… Ente… Enter… Esch… NA     
#> 2 GG_OTU_2 Bacteria Cyanobacteria  Nostocophycideae   Nost… Nosto… Doli… NA     
#> 3 GG_OTU_3 Archaea  Euryarchaeota  Methanomicrobia    Meth… Metha… Meth… NA     
#> 4 GG_OTU_4 Bacteria Firmicutes     Clostridia         Hala… Halan… Hala… Halana…
#> 5 GG_OTU_5 Bacteria Proteobacteria Gammaproteobacter… Ente… Enter… Esch… NA

The same file can be imported as a TreeSummarizedExperiment. Rows of a TSE represent features, columns represent samples, rowData() holds feature annotations and colData() holds sample metadata.

tse <- mia::importBIOM(biom_file)

# This bundled example contains these seven ranks, in this order.
colnames(SummarizedExperiment::rowData(tse)) <- c(
  "Kingdom", "Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Family", "Genus", "Species"
)

tse_rec <- recipe(tse)
head(dar::tax_table(tse_rec))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 8
#>   taxa_id  Kingdom     Phylum            Class        Order Family Genus Species
#>   <chr>    <chr>       <chr>             <chr>        <chr> <chr>  <chr> <chr>  
#> 1 GG_OTU_1 k__Bacteria p__Proteobacteria c__Gammapro… o__E… f__En… g__E… s__    
#> 2 GG_OTU_2 k__Bacteria p__Cyanobacteria  c__Nostocop… o__N… f__No… g__D… s__    
#> 3 GG_OTU_3 k__Archaea  p__Euryarchaeota  c__Methanom… o__M… f__Me… g__M… s__    
#> 4 GG_OTU_4 k__Bacteria p__Firmicutes     c__Clostrid… o__H… f__Ha… g__H… s__Hal…
#> 5 GG_OTU_5 k__Bacteria p__Proteobacteria c__Gammapro… o__E… f__En… g__E… s__

The rank relabeling above is specific to this file. Inspect the annotations in your own data instead of assigning rank names by position without checking their meaning. A TSE input is converted internally to phyloseq; if the intended abundance table is not the default assay, select it explicitly with mia::convertToPhyloseq(..., assay.type = "your_assay") before creating the recipe.

For other formats, consult the importers’ documentation rather than treating all formats as equivalent:

  • phyloseq::import_qiime() reads legacy QIIME tables; mia::importQIIME2() reads QIIME 2 artifacts.
  • phyloseq::import_mothur() and mia::importMothur() read the supported mothur files.
  • mia::importMetaPhlAn() reads MetaPhlAn abundance profiles.

For example, open the installed help with help("importQIIME2", package = "mia") or help("import_biom", package = "phyloseq").

Check the measurement scale

An abundance matrix can contain raw read counts, proportions, percentages or other transformed values. These are not interchangeable inputs. In particular, MetaPhlAn relative-abundance profiles are not raw read counts. Neither importing them nor converting their container makes them suitable for a count-based model; rounding percentages does not recover read counts.

Check the provenance and assay units, not just whether values happen to be integers. Retain raw counts when they are available and choose a method whose input requirements match the measurements. Missing values are also distinct from observed zeros.

For QC and filtering, continue with Quality control and preprocessing. For formulas, target variables and engine compatibility, see Statistical models and contrasts.
